examples.title: Filtering Rows
examples.description: Keep only the rows that match a condition
examples.markdown:
## Filtering rows with a boolean mask

`cones['Flavor'] == 'chocolate'` is True or False for each row. Putting it inside `cones[...]` keeps the rows where it is True.

Watch the index on the left: the kept rows keep their original labels, 1 and 3.
cells:
# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pd.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Only the chocolate cones
chocolate = cones[cones['Flavor'] == 'chocolate']
chocolate

examples.title: Two Conditions
examples.markdown:
## Combining conditions

Join conditions with `&` (and) or `|` (or). Each condition needs its own parentheses, because `&` binds more tightly than `>`.
cells:
# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pd.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Chocolate cones under $5
cheap_chocolate = cones[(cones['Flavor'] == 'chocolate') & (cones['Price'] < 5)]
cheap_chocolate

## `query`

cones

examples.title: Rows and Columns with loc
examples.description: Pick rows by condition and columns by name
examples.markdown:
## `loc[rows, columns]`

`loc` takes a row selector and a column selector at once. Here the rows come from a condition and the columns from a list.

examples.title: Sorting Rows
examples.markdown:
## `sort_values`

`ascending=False` puts the largest first. Rows move as a whole, and each keeps its index label, so you can see where it came from.

})
cones

examples.title: Average per Group
examples.markdown:
## `groupby` and `mean`

`groupby('Flavor')` puts rows with the same flavor together; `['Price'].mean()` then averages each group's prices. The flavors become the result's index.
cells:
# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pd.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

examples.title: Merging Tables
examples.description: Match rows of two tables on a key
examples.markdown:
## `merge`

`merge` matches rows whose `Flavor` is equal in both tables. By default (`how='inner'`) rows without a match on the other side are dropped: strawberry has no rating, and nobody sells cookie dough.
cells:
# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pd.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

examples.title: Keeping Every Row
examples.description: A left merge keeps unmatched rows
examples.markdown:
## `how='left'`

A left merge keeps every row of the left table. Where the right table has no match, its columns are NaN, shown blank.

cones

examples.title: Pivot Table
examples.description: Summarize two columns as a grid
examples.markdown:
## `pivot_table`

Flavors become the rows, colors the columns, and each cell is the average price of the cones that fall in it. Empty combinations are NaN, shown blank.
cells:
# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pd.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

grid = cones.pivot_table(index='Flavor', columns='Color', values='Price', aggfunc='mean')
grid
